usage: Person + 을/를 + 사랑하다 is the basic pattern.
The bare casual form 사랑해 is the most famous way to say 'I love you'.
examples: Casual form used between close people and couples.
My parents loved each other a lot
사랑하셨어요 adds honorific 시 for parents.
nuance: 사랑하다 is the standard verb for romantic, family, and deep affection. It is a regular 하다 verb, so it becomes 사랑해요, not 사랑하요. Koreans say 사랑해 less casually than English speakers say 'love you' — it carries real weight.
mistakes: Writing 사랑하요 instead of 사랑해요 — 하다 always contracts to 해요.
Using 에 instead of 을/를 for the person you love.

usage: 미워하지 마 is the casual 'don't hate me'.
nuance: 미워하다 means to feel hatred or resentment toward someone, and is the verb form built from the adjective 밉다 (to be hateful). It is a regular 하다 verb, so it conjugates as 미워해요. It is strong, so for mild dislike Koreans prefer 싫어하다.
mistakes: Confusing 미워하다 (to hate a person) with 싫어하다 (to dislike something).

usage: Object + 을/를 + 그리워하다 for missing a place or person.
Use the past 했어요 to say you missed someone.
examples: Past tense, talking about absent people.
Don't miss your family too much
Casual 하지 마 form of comfort.
nuance: 그리워하다 is the action verb 'to miss / long for', built from the adjective 그립다 (to be missed). Use 그립다 to describe a feeling about yourself (고향이 그리워요 = I feel homesick) and 그리워하다 to describe someone actively missing something. It is a regular 하다 verb.
mistakes: Confusing the adjective 그립다 (it is missed) with the verb 그리워하다 (to miss).
Using 보고 싶다 (want to see) and 그리워하다 interchangeably — 보고 싶다 is more everyday.

usage: 소원을 빌다 = to make a wish, a very common collocation.
행운을 빌어요 is the everyday way to say 'good luck'.
examples: I made a wish at New Year
I pray for my family's health
시험 잘 보라고 행운을 빌어 줄게요
I'll wish you luck on your test
빌어 주다 = to wish on someone's behalf.
nuance: 빌다 means to pray, wish, or plead for something, as in 소원을 빌다 (make a wish) and 행운을 빌다 (wish luck). It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, and ㅅ endings, so the formal form is 빕니다 and the future is 빌 거예요 (no doubled ㄹ). Note that 빌다 can also mean 'to borrow' in older usage, but modern Korean uses 빌리다 for borrowing.
mistakes: Writing the formal form as 빌습니다 — the ㄹ drops, so it is 빕니다.
Confusing 빌다 (to pray / wish) with 빌리다 (to borrow).

usage: I raise a puppy / I have a dog
키우다 is the normal verb for keeping a pet.
Past 키웠어요, the ㅜ stem contracts with 어.
examples: The everyday way to say you keep a pet.
키워 주셨어요 adds honorific 시 and 주다 (for me).
I want to grow plants well
nuance: 키우다 means to raise or bring up — children, pets, and plants — and also to grow something bigger (실력을 키우다 = build up skills). The stem ends in ㅜ, so 키우 + 어 contracts to 키워, giving 키워요 and past 키웠어요. For pets, Koreans default to 키우다 rather than 가지다.
mistakes: Writing 키우어요 instead of the contracted 키워요.
Using 가지다 (to have) for a pet instead of the natural 키우다.

usage: 머리를 기르다 = to grow one's hair out.
Past 길렀어요 shows the 르 irregular doubling.
examples: 기르다 is used for hair, beard, and nails.
기르다 also means to cultivate habits or skills.
nuance: 기르다 means to grow, raise, or cultivate — hair, plants, animals, and even habits or abilities. It is a 르-irregular verb: before an 아/어 ending the 르 becomes ㄹㄹ, so 기르 + 어 turns into 길러, and the past is 길렀어요. It overlaps with 키우다, but 기르다 is preferred for hair and beard.
mistakes: Writing the past as 기르었어요 — the 르 irregular makes it 길렀어요.
Forgetting the doubled ㄹ: the casual form is 길러, not 기러.

usage: I give birth to a baby
아기를 낳다 = to have a baby.
I gave birth to a son
Past 낳았어요; the ㅎ stays and ㅏ takes 았.
examples: My older sister gave birth to a daughter
낳다 is also used for animals.
I want to have two children
낳고 싶어요 = want to give birth.
nuance: 낳다 means to give birth to or bear (a child or young). It is a regular consonant-stem verb — the ㅎ is kept, so it is 낳아요 and 낳았어요, NOT 나아요. Do not confuse it with the similar-looking 낫다 (to recover / be better), which is ㅅ-irregular and becomes 나아요.
mistakes: Confusing 낳다 (give birth) with 낫다 (recover) — they sound alike but conjugate differently.
Dropping the ㅎ and writing 나아요; the correct polite form is 낳아요.

usage: Person + 을/를 + 닮다, usually in the past tense 닮았어요.
examples: The baby looks a lot like the dad
닮다 covers both looks and personality.
My personality resembles my older brother's
nuance: 닮다 means to resemble or take after someone, in looks or character. Korean usually states resemblance in the past tense — 닮았어요 ('looks like') describes a present fact, much like English 'looks like'. The object of resemblance takes 을/를, or you can pair people with 하고/와/과.
mistakes: Saying 닮아요 for 'looks like' — Koreans normally use the past 닮았어요 for a present resemblance.
Using 같다 (to be the same) when you mean only a resemblance, which is 닮다.

usage: Subject + 이/가 + 잘 어울리다 = suits well.
I get along well with friends
어울리다 also means to mingle / get along.
examples: Complimenting how something looks on someone.
These shoes go well with the skirt
하고 어울리다 = to match / go with.
I mixed well with the new coworkers
Past 어울렸어요 in the 'get along' sense.
nuance: 어울리다 has two everyday meanings: (1) to suit or look good on someone, and (2) to mingle, match, or get along with others. The thing that suits takes 이/가, and the person or item it matches takes 하고/와/과. The stem ends in ㅣ, so 어울리 + 어 contracts to 어울려, giving 어울려요 and past 어울렸어요.
mistakes: Using 을/를 for what suits you — say 옷이 어울려요 (이/가), not 옷을 어울려요.
Writing 어울리어요 instead of the contracted 어울려요.
